description_full: Ecolab Inc. provides water, hygiene, and infection prevention solutions and services in the United States and internationally. The company operates through four segments: Global Water, Global Institutional & Specialty, Global Pest Elimination, and Global Life Sciences. The Global Water segment offers water treatment and process applications, and cleaning and sanitizing solutions to manufacturing, food and beverage processing, transportation, chemical, primary metals and mining, power generation, global refining, petrochemical, pulp and paper industries. The Global Institutional & Specialty segment provides cleaning and sanitizing products to the foodservice, healthcare, hospitality, lodging, government, education and retail industries. The Global Pest Elimination segment provides pest elimination services to detect, prevent, and eliminate pests comprising rodents and insects in full-service and quick-service restaurants, food and beverage processors, hotels, grocery operations, and other commercial segments, including education, life sciences, and healthcare. The Global Life Sciences segment provides cleaning and contamination control solutions to pharmaceutical and personal care manufacturers. It offers its products under the Ecolab, Kay, Purolite, and Bioquell brand names. The company sells its products through field sales and corporate account personnel, distributors, and dealers. Ecolab Inc. was founded in 1923 and is headquartered in Saint Paul, Minnesota.

financial_summary: Ecolab Inc. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $84.3B market cap on $16.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $1.9B in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 8.9×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 17% operating margin runs 7pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.30x).
It accounts for 1.0% of sector revenue and 1.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 12% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 22% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.24 vs 5y 0.94), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $348.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash, 43% in the 2022 bear market and 41% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $81.16 (margin of safety -270%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $61.72 to $107 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 40.9 vs 16.5, EV/EBITDA 23.1 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 44.3 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 25% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 21 covering analysts target $331 on average, 10% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 9.0%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.30).
It converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.42x.
ROE of 21% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.3% of revenue on R&D and 0.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.2x net debt to EBITDA ($646.2M of cash against $8.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 8.9x.
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.3% over 3 years, 6.4% over 5 years and 1.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (6.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 94%.
Insider trading is two-way: 3 purchases and 3 sales over the past year, net $6.0M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (0.9% in buybacks and 1.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 6.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 48,000 employees, each generates about $335K of revenue, 0.5x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 6.5% a year.
That works out to $40K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.2M (15x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
